title: Adolescents’ Perceptions of Cannabis-Related Risk and Harm, Attitudes and Social Norms Following Cannabis Decriminalisation in South Africa: A Cross-Sectional Study Among High School Learners in Tshwane
content: A shift in cannabis legislation may influence adolescents' perceptions of cannabis-related risk, harm, and social acceptability. This study explored adolescents' perceptions of cannabis-related risk and harm, attitudes towards cannabis use, perceived social norms, and the perceived influence of cannabis decriminalisation among high school learners in Tshwane, South Africa. A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted among 412 learners in Grades 8–12 attending selected public high schools. Data were collected using a structured self-administered questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression. Approximately one-third of learners reported current or previous cannabis use. Most learners reported that cannabis legalisation had no effect on their views or attitudes towards cannabis, while learners also reported cannabis use among close friends and family members. Perceptions of cannabis-related risk, harm, and social norms were significantly associated with selected demographic, behavioural, social, and legalisation-related factors in bivariate analyses; however, none remained independently associated following multivariable adjustment. The findings support adolescent-centred prevention and health promotion strategies that strengthen cannabis-related risk awareness and address social contexts associated with adolescents' attitudes and perceptions.
